chapter: Race, rock and the craft of vocalese
title: Teaching singers: listen, and Judith's Wendell Culley solo
summary: His jazz poem is Listen; he says Judith sings Wendell Culley's solo exactly, whereas most singers are lazy.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You’re remarkable. How do you go about – you’ve influenced many vocalists. I think that there’s a lineage that certainly comes through you and goes on. How do you train other vocalists? For instance, I know, in your group, you’ve had different baritones – baritone singers. How do you indoctrinate them into the Hendricks concept.

I use what I said in my short jazz poem. I wrote the shortest jazz poem. You know that jazz poem. “Listen.” I tell them that if you listen, and you hear the horn, and you sing what you hear, then I don’t have to tell you anything. You got it right. One of the students that I’ve heard actually do that is Judith. Judith sang – she sings the solo of Wendell Culley on Little Darlin’. We played in the south of France. A man of about 60 years old came backstage and says, “Incroyable, incroyable. She sings ze solo exactly ze way Wendell Culley play it. It is incroyable.” He really – he knew that solo, and she sings that solo right down to the tee. That’s the way it should be done. Most singers are lazy, and they just approximate. That’s terrible. I hate that, because that – you’re only halfway through the work. Do the rest of it. Learn it and do it well. Judith: He doesn’t approve of anyone.
